If [MATH: A] is true, then [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is [MATH: \text{______________}.]

Which of the following could fill in the blank space above to make a true statement?

1. always true
2. always false
3. sometimes false

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The statement [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is true unless [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is false.

Let's break this down into cases:

  • When [MATH: A = \textrm T] and [MATH: B = \textrm T,] we have [MATH: (A⇒B)|≡(T⇒T); ≡T.]

  • When [MATH: A = \textrm T] and [MATH: B = \textrm F,] we have [MATH: (A⇒B)|≡(T⇒F); ≡F.]

Therefore, if [MATH: A] is true, then [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{sometimes false}}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A conditional statement (or implication) is a mathematical statement that takes the form

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q,]

Content:
or equivalently,

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] if [MATH: P,] then [MATH: Q.]

Content:
Symbolically, it can be written as [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q,] where [MATH: P] is called the antecedent (or hypothesis) and [MATH: Q] is called the consequent (or conclusion).

Content:
The truth table for [MATH: P \Rightarrow Q] is shown below.

Content:
| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \, P \Rightarrow Q \,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{black} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{black} \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \color{black} \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \color{black} \textrm T] |

Content:
Intuitively, an implication can be viewed as a "promise" that whenever [MATH: P] is true, [MATH: Q] is also true. The implication is true unless the promise is broken, i.e., [MATH: P] is true, and [MATH: Q] is false.

Content:
We'll discuss the intuition behind implications in more detail later in the lesson.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Truth Values of Implications

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: A] is true, then [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is [MATH: \text{______________}.]

Which of the following could fill in the blank space above to make a true statement?

1. always true
2. always false
3. sometimes false

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The statement [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is true unless [MATH: A] is true and [MATH: B] is false.

Let's break this down into cases:

- When [MATH: A = \textrm T] and [MATH: B = \textrm T,] we have
[MATH: (A⇒B)|≡(T⇒T); ≡T.]
- When [MATH: A = \textrm T] and [MATH: B = \textrm F,] we have
[MATH: (A⇒B)|≡(T⇒F); ≡F.]

Therefore, if [MATH: A] is true, then [MATH: A \Rightarrow B] is [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{sometimes false}}.]

The complete truth table for [MATH: A\Rightarrow B] is shown below:

| [MATH: \,A\,] | [MATH: \,B\,] | [MATH: \,A \Rightarrow B\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm T}] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
